title: The Traffic Layer
lede: Everything between your users and your servers. These two concepts arrived early, from the phase 0 course — which is the territory telling you that scalability is not a later chapter. The phase itself is a revisit with production scars, and you buy nothing for it.
source: Notes from Udemy: Software Architecture & Design of Modern Large Scale Systems — Michael Pogrebinsky

concepts.lede: Distributes traffic across servers to prevent overload — and quietly buys you three other quality attributes at the same time.

items: **Scalability** — add or remove servers with load
**Availability** — health monitoring, so traffic only reaches operational servers
**Performance** — slightly more latency, massively more throughput
**Maintainability** — rolling updates: take servers offline one at a time
**DNS load balancing** — basic. No health monitoring, no security.
**Hardware / software LB** — active health checks, intelligent routing, hides backend topology
**Global server LB (GSLB)** — DNS plus routing by user location and health; this is what makes disaster recovery real
**Cloud** — AWS ELB (Application, Network, Gateway, Classic), GCP Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer
**GSLB** — AWS Route 53, AWS Global Accelerator, GCP Cloud DNS, Azure Traffic Manager

blocks.call: The maintainability benefit is the one people forget: a balancer is what turns a release from a maintenance window into a rolling update.

cards: Traffic spikes and one server dies. Users report errors. What pattern solves both problems, and which two features?
A load balancer — horizontal scaling for the spike, health checks to route around the dead server.
You need to deploy a new version without downtime. How does a load balancer help?
Rolling updates — take servers offline one at a time while the LB routes to healthy ones.
Your European users experience high latency hitting US servers. What LB type fixes this?
Global server load balancing — routes by user geography and server health.
concepts.drill: Year One · One box out of four

concepts.lede: Reduces the latency caused by physical distance, by caching content on edge servers close to the user.

items: Lower latency and faster load times
DDoS protection — the attack is absorbed at the edge, not at your origin

rows: The CDN fetches from origin on a cache miss; you configure a TTL
The first request for uncached content is slow, and TTL bounds staleness
You upload content to the CDN proactively
Users always get the latest version

items: Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront, GCP CDN, Azure CDN

cards: Your video platform users in Asia experience 3s load times because the server is in Virginia. What fixes this?
A CDN — cache content on edge servers geographically closer to users.
Your marketing site content rarely changes and you want minimal maintenance. Pull or push?
Pull — the CDN fetches on a cache miss, managed with a TTL.
Your pricing page must update instantly worldwide after a product launch. Pull or push?
Push — proactively upload so every edge has the latest version.
